title: 700,000 People, One Pope, and a Giant Open-Air Mass in Paris
summary:
Imagine standing in a crowd of 700,000 people. That's about the population of a whole big city — all gathered in one square in Paris. On Saturday, that's exactly what happened at the Place de la Concorde, where Pope Leo XIV led an open-air Mass.

The Pope rode down the famous Champs-Élysées Avenue in his open-topped popemobile, waving to crowds. Then he celebrated Mass from a special altar. It was the second day of his four-day visit to France.

In his speech, the Pope had a special message for young people. He called them "today's Church" and said: "How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities." He also told Catholics not to keep their faith to themselves, but to "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed."

Lots of important people came. France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Brigitte Macron, the president's wife, were there. President Emmanuel Macron did not attend — France has strict rules about keeping church and government separate.

Earlier, the Pope visited a center that helps refugees. He also warned about the dangers of artificial intelligence. Big crowds are expected for the rest of his trip.
why_it_matters: The Pope's message tells young people that their energy and enthusiasm matter, and it reminds us how different countries handle the balance between religion and government.

background_read: The Pope (the leader of the Roman Catholic Church, which has more than a billion members around the world) travels to other countries to meet believers and lead services.
A Mass is a Catholic religious service. It is usually held in a church, but for very big crowds it is held outdoors in a large public square, just like this one in Paris.
The Place de la Concorde (a huge square in Paris with a famous fountain and stone pillar) and the Champs-Élysées (a wide, famous avenue in the city) are well-known Paris landmarks the Pope rode past.
France has a long tradition of keeping religion and government separate, which is why the president stayed away from the religious ceremony.
